claims.text: Premelting in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles initiates through thermally activated surface diffusion.
Surface diffusion produces a disordered, liquid-like surface layer.
The liquid-like surface layer progressively thickens and coalesces into complete melting.
The high surface-to-volume ratio of the nanoparticles promotes surface premelting.
Complex local chemical interactions in multi-principal-element alloys contribute to the premelting behavior.
Variations in elemental surface segregation reduce the energy barrier for surface disordering.
The starting FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles have uniform composition and crystallinity.
An elevated surface-to-volume ratio and heterogeneous elemental distribution lower the local melting barrier at the nanoparticle surface.
Thermally activated diffusion initiates a premelting layer that grows with temperature.
The growing premelting layer eventually spans the nanoparticle and produces complete melting.
A thin, disordered surface layer will emerge below the bulk melting point.
Increasing temperature will cause the disordered surface layer to thicken until full melting occurs.
Premelting and melting will produce detectable changes in diffraction patterns, diffusional behavior, or calorimetric signals.
Larger particle size may alter the proposed behavior by reducing surface-to-volume effects.
Significant surface passivation may impede surface diffusion and alter the proposed premelting behavior.

contradictions.description: The starting particles are described as compositionally uniform, while the mechanism invokes a heterogeneous elemental distribution as an existing cause of barrier lowering. This could be reconciled if heterogeneity develops during heating, but that temporal distinction is not stated clearly.
